rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: ReuseGR: Offline--Online Decoupled Generative Retrieval via Adaptive Prefix Reuse
papers.authors: Xujing Wang, Yufeng Chen, Boxuan Zhang, Chao Wei, Cai Xu, Jie Zhao, Weiru Zhang, Wei Zhao, Ziyu Guan
papers.summary: Teams putting generative retrieval into production should read this: it shows how to reuse large-model compute per query while leaving personalization to a small online model, and it is backed by an online A/B test. The same query is searched by many people every day, so generating a full Semantic ID from scratch for each request repeats work. ReuseGR splits the job in two. Offline, a large model generates a set of SID prefixes per query, shared by all requests with that query. Online, a small model picks prefixes using the current user's history and completes the remaining tokens. On a search-advertising dataset, assuming prefixes are already cached, it matches the recall of running the large model fully online, with 57.7% lower online latency. In an online A/B test, CTR rose 0.93% relative to the small-model baseline.

papers.title: Diverse-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhipeng Yi, Xinyu Lin, Minxuan Shan, Zipeng Chen, Yujiao Zhao, Chuanyu Xu, Wenjie Wang
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), where the student generates on its own and a teacher gives a full probability distribution at each position, makes generative recommenders train faster, but the student drifts further and further toward popular items. The bias comes from two places: the teacher's probabilities already favor the SIDs of popular items, and the student rarely generates the SIDs of unpopular items, so those paths get almost no supervision. HERO first splits items into popular and unpopular groups by how often they appear in the training data, trains one teacher from scratch on each, and freezes both. During distillation, each training example goes to the teacher that matches the group of the item the user actually clicked. The student generates a few SIDs itself with beam search and, at every position, moves toward that teacher's full probability distribution. When the true item is unpopular, its true SID is added as an extra path, and the student matches the unpopular-item teacher at every position along it too. Only the student is served. In a 15-day A/B test on the Guess What You Like module of the 1688 homepage, GMV rose 3.412%.

papers.title: Large Language Model as Universal Retriever in Industrial-Scale Recommender System
papers.authors: Junguang Jiang, Yanwen Huang, Liu Bin, Xiaoyu Kong, Xinhang Li
papers.summary: In this CIKM paper from Alibaba's Taobao and Tmall Group, one large language model handles click retrieval, per-scenario retrieval, long-tail retrieval, interest exploration and retrieval with a search query at the same time, and overall does better than the multi-task retrieval models common in industry. The user's history and the goal of this retrieval are written into one input. The LLM outputs several user vectors in a single forward pass. Each of tens of millions of candidate items is scored by its highest inner product with those vectors, and the top-scoring set is kept. On 9 retrieval objectives in industrial data, average R@1000 is 11.0% higher (relative) than the strongest multi-task baseline; in an online A/B test on an advertising platform, advertising revenue rose 3.01%. ==What really matters is one model that switches retrieval objectives on instruction==: a new objective close to the learned ones can be tried by changing one sentence.

papers.title: Utility-Aware Generative Recommendation: Utility-Enriched Semantic Codes and Utility-Guided Decoding
papers.authors: Yang Hu, Duo Wang, Ning Li, Kang Li, Junda She, Chengcheng Guo, Kuo Cai, Bin Liu, Youhua Liu, Xiaoshuang Chen
papers.summary: This Kuaishou paper adds video utility to two places in generative recommendation that used to look only at content and probability. 3 bits inside the last SID token record the video's utility tier: 7 ascending boundaries cut one utility statistic (such as historical click rate) into 8 tiers. At every beam-search step a small module reads the decoder hidden state, predicts behaviors such as watching and liking for each candidate. The normalized predictions are summed with weights into a utility score. That score is scaled by a coefficient and added to the log generation probability, and pruning uses the total. This is needed because common generative recommenders build SIDs from content alone, so a video people usually finish and one most people swipe away get nearly the same code whenever their content is similar. Beam search then prunes by generation probability alone, so a high-utility candidate can be cut at some middle token, and later reranking cannot bring it back. It is fully deployed at Kuaishou, lifting video watch time by 0.206%. ==Utility used at the pruning step works better than utility used only for reranking after generation==.

papers.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Zhuosheng Liu, Yihan Wu, Ziyun Xu, Xiaoxuan Liu, Longfei Yun, Kevin Han, Mingze Gao, Pengfei Wang, Junfeng Pan, Wenjie F...
papers.summary: This Meta paper gives every creator its own token in the language model's vocabulary and uses it in place of the SID. The reason is simple: an SID is a many-to-one code, so several creators share one SID, and even when the model generates the right SID it still has to guess which of those creators the user wants. On Meta's creator recommendation data, swapping only the token layer lifts the share of cases where the user's next engaged creator appears in the top 15 from 23.58% to 43.41%. The SID pipeline's per-user inference cost is about 2.7 times the new method's. ==The bottleneck is the SID layer, not the language model==. The price is that every token needs enough training examples, so the authors use it only for head creators.

papers.title: PFA: Attention Can Be Progressively Focused in Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Pengjie Zhou, Weiqin Yang, Haibo Xing, Hao Deng, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: The authors at Alibaba found that when a generative recommender decodes with beam search, attention concentrates on a few past behaviors as decoding proceeds, and which behaviors matter stays largely the same from step to step. Building on this, PFA picks the important history once for the whole decode, instead of having every beam pick it again at every step. It attends to the full history as usual at the first decoding step. At the second step it pools the beams' attention over the history, weighted by generation probability, into one shared ranking of important behaviors, and it shrinks the number of kept behaviors by a fixed ratio at each later step. In an online A/B test on an e-commerce ads platform, the user history grew from 128 to 512 behaviors, revenue rose 3.76%. Response time stayed below that of feeding the full history directly.

papers.title: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising
papers.authors: Yatong Xiao, Yibo Sheng, Lixiang Wang, Mingjie Sun, Yunhao Sha, Pengfei Zhang, Shengyu Wang, Peng Wang, Wenjin Wu, Peng ...
papers.summary: Kuaishou made three changes to GR4AD, its deployed generative ad retrieval system, and the result, GR4AD-X, raises online ad revenue by a cumulative 3.07% over GR4AD. All three target the same mismatch: the model picks ads by generation probability, while the platform cares about revenue. The top ten ads by generation probability and the top ten by eCPM barely overlap, with a hit rate of only about 0.02. The first change keeps the two nearest first-level cluster centers for each ad, so it can still be retrieved when one prefix is pruned. The second skips a bigger backbone and instead feeds in twenty-odd extra user-profile and context features from the ranking system and widens the embeddings of key features. The third estimates a revenue value for each SID prefix, namely the mean revenue of the ads beneath it. During pruning, RRF combines each prefix's positions in the probability ranking and in the value ranking into one score, and candidates are cut by that score. ==The changes were stacked one at a time in online tests==.

papers.title: UGR: Unified Generative Ranking for Heterogeneous E-commerce Recommendation
papers.authors: Zonghe Shao, Huabin Chen, Sitong Lu, Fangmei Zhu, Yingcai Ma, Ge Fan, Jinguo Gao, Wei Shi, Yanfang Liu, Huiping Chu
papers.summary: Taobao's generative ranking framework UGR has one generative model directly produce the screen the user finally sees. The roughly one thousand organic, ad and other-business candidates of a request go to the model together, and it generates the final list item by item, instead of each business ranking its own items and a blending stage stitching them together. That stitching step is the old problem: the blender inserts other content into the generator's list, positions and context change, and the order the model learned no longer holds. In an online A/B test on Guess You Like, transaction volume rose 3.29%; when the same model ranks only organic items and hands them to the old blender, transaction volume rises only 2.84%, and ==the gap is the value of unified generation itself==.

papers.title: Where Beam Search Loses Top-Ranked Items:First-Step Coverage in Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Heng Yao, Hanwei Zhu
papers.summary: A generative recommender uses beam search to produce a SID one token at a time, and the usual way to miss fewer good results is to widen every step at once. This paper checks six full-test settings of TIGER one by one: every result that the model's own scores put in the top 10, but that beam search pruned, was lost at the very first step. So the cheaper move is to concentrate width on the first step and narrow the later ones. With this allocation, about half the prefix budget (the total number of prefixes kept across steps) reproduces the top 10 of a beam twice as wide, in the same order, with no retraining. ==Beam width should go to the step where results get lost==.

papers.title: ZeroGR: Filtering-First Constrained Decoding for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Xiangrui Yang, Jiawei Yang, Liang Zeng, Daqian Ding, Ziqian Liu, Bing Tian, Cheng Peng, Yunfeng Zhao, Fangyu Zhang, Jiaq...
papers.summary: Engineering teams serving generative recommenders should read this: it shows that most constrained-decoding compute goes to candidates that will be discarded, and gives a filter-first system implementation. Generative recommenders emit item codes one token at a time, and every step must keep the code pointing at an item that really exists in the catalog. The usual approach scores every possible next token and then filters out the invalid ones, so most of those scores are wasted. The authors first check: filtering before scoring returns about 99.9% of the same items. ZeroGR does two things for this. First, it slices the filtering index by decoding step, stored sparsely when a step has few valid candidates and densely when it has many, which saves GPU memory. Second, within a step every beam gets the same number of candidate slots, and filtering and scoring read and write the slots directly instead of first packing candidates into a compact list; only then do fewer scores become a real speedup. The combined filtering, scoring and candidate selection stage runs up to 9.9 times faster than representative baselines.

papers.title: Numerical Embeddings for CTR Prediction: A Taxonomy, Unified Benchmark, and Open-Source FuxiCTR Extension
papers.authors: Heng Yao, Hanwei Zhu, Tianying Liu, Yulou Shu, Siyun Hou
papers.summary: There are a dozen or so ways for a CTR model to turn numerical features such as prices and counts into vectors, and in one fair comparison no single method wins everywhere. This used to be hard to compare, because papers differ in preprocessing and training pipelines. This paper puts 18 of them into one codebase with the same tuning budget and compares them across several datasets and backbones. DEER has the best overall rank, but it does not win everywhere: change the dataset or the backbone and the leader can change. When the inputs switch from standardized values back to their original scale, the winner changes in 11 of 27 settings. Accuracy and inference latency also do not rise and fall together. So how to encode numerical features has to be re-tested on your own data and backbone.

papers.title: Auditing a Model-Hub Benchmark: Data Quality, Training Budgets, and Side Information in HuggingBench
papers.authors: Michal Podstawski
papers.summary: Worth reading for anyone who evaluates recommenders, because the problem it uncovers is not in the models but in how the data files map onto each other. In HuggingBench, the public benchmark for recommending Hugging Face models and datasets, three of the four knowledge graphs that describe the items have their item IDs matched wrongly, so knowledge-graph recommenders have been reading another item's facts as this item's. The files pass the usual key and range checks; only a join by content reveals the mismatch. After the fix, every knowledge-graph method improves, with mean recall up by as much as 73%. The benchmark also ships each item's text description, which no reported method uses. Linear models that use this text train in minutes on a CPU and beat the best reported recall by 17%.

papers.title: Improving Ads Ranking Models with Auxiliary Supervision: Techniques and Insights
papers.authors: Nikhil Bhale, Apurva Pathak, SaiSujithKumarReddy MarapaReddy, Xiao Yin, Prateek Bhansali
papers.summary: Ad CVR models are trained on conversion events such as purchases and installs, but conversions are rare, and about half of the training samples in this Meta model have no conversion label. The paper fills the gap with other signals: how long a user looked at the ad before clicking, add-to-cart events, the semantics of the ad content and similar signals all become auxiliary tasks trained alongside the main task, at no extra online inference cost. Auxiliary signals are often noisy. The most effective fix is called LaCo, and it works on yes-or-no signals, such as whether the user added the item to the cart. LaCo combines several such signals with AND, OR and XOR, picks the combination that best matches real conversions, above all the one with the fewest false positives, and trains on it as a new label. It lowers offline NE by 0.25%. After these changes shipped together with other improvements, advertiser conversion volume rose with statistical significance in A/B tests. For teams doing conversion prediction, making auxiliary labels accurate pays off more than piling on more auxiliary tasks.

papers.title: PACT: Defending Recommendation against Promotional News Rewriting via Attack-Diverse Score Consistency
papers.authors: Chongxian Chen, Fan Mo, Xin Fan, Hayato Yamana
papers.summary: A news publisher can ask an LLM to make a headline more eye-catching without changing a single fact, and the ranking still goes up. This paper's defense is called PACT, and it changes only training. Before training, many different LLMs and rewriting methods produce a batch of rewritten headlines for each training article. During training, each time an article comes up, one rewrite is drawn at random, and the model is asked to give the original and the rewritten headline about the same score for the same user. The deployed model keeps its architecture, with no filtering and no added latency. Against the strongest rewriting attack, LANCE, the share of user and article pairs pushed up the ranking on NRMS drops from 61.4% to 55.4%: the attack is weakened, not removed.

papers.title: When Category Means Move: A Paired-Support Audit of Recommendation Logs with Random Insertions
papers.authors: Yu Zhang, Zhihan Wang, Yuhang Lu, Shuai Li
papers.summary: Many teams decide which content categories to promote from the average watch ratio per category in their recommendation logs; this paper measures how far that dashboard is skewed by the serving policy. The authors use KuaiRand, a public Kuaishou dataset that randomly swaps one video into some recommendation lists; those impressions are not picked by the policy and serve as a reference. On the same users and videos, category means in the normal log are much higher across the board, yet the order of categories differs only moderately. Subtracting each user's own average and then anchoring to the overall random-impression mean cuts the average gap between each category and the reference by 80%. But if both sides are first leveled and one compares only how far each category sits above or below the average, the gap shrinks by only 21%, and the ranking does not reliably improve.

papers.title: Lightweight Ranking Heads: Accelerating Multi-Task Experimentation in Production Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Sanjay Surendranath Girija, Aniruddh Nath, Li Wei, Yanhao Jiang, Shawn Andrews, Lukasz Heldt, Yi Wu, Aditya Mahajan, Moh...
papers.summary: The bigger a multi-task ranking model gets, the slower it becomes to add a new prediction target. YouTube's answer keeps the new target out of the main model and makes it a small prediction head on top of the shared layers (the paper calls it a Light Head). It only reads the shared layers' output, sends no gradient down, and is reset at the start of every training run, and every ranking model reads it from the same config. With the framework, a full experiment cycle covering the ranker and a downstream model shrank from 24 days to 11. The cost is an AUC about 0.01 lower than a fully trained head on data-rich tasks such as clicks.

papers.title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
papers.authors: Shivam Swarup, Divya Prakash Shrivastava, Rakesh Thakur
papers.summary: Shilling detection almost always reports a single AUROC, and that number cannot say when the detector can be trusted. This paper builds an auditing framework to check exactly that. Common fake-account injections are all caught. An attack that copies real users changes everything: each fake account copies every movie a real user rated and adds 1 to 3 target movies, and on MovieLens-1M AUROC falls to coin-flip level. Yet comparing the largest overlap of rated items between accounts in the raw records reaches AUROC 0.92–0.97. The problem is the embedding: LightGCN sees only which items were rated and then smooths similar accounts together through graph propagation, so this signal is lost.

papers.title: Learning to Rank Explanations for Recommendation with Language Models
papers.authors: Ben Kabongo, Vincent Guigue
papers.summary: When picking recommendation reasons for a user, earlier methods often fail to beat a simple baseline that only counts which statements appear most in the user's history. The task is to take the short statements extracted and merged from all reviews of an item and pick the few most likely to resonate with this user. LMStaR uses a fine-tuned text embedding model and treats this as retrieval: one encoder reads the user's earlier reviews and the item's information, another reads each statement. In training the two are fine-tuned together so that statements from the review the user actually wrote for this item rank first. On Amazon Beauty, Amazon Toys and Yelp, its first-ranked reason is the most accurate on all three, 1.06 to 8.25 points above CLER, the strongest earlier method.

papers.title: BrowseFlow: Sparse Event Flow Matching for Generative User Simulation
papers.authors: Yitian Pang, Jiayi Zhang, Zhenjia Ma, Xiaowei Yue, Dagui Chen, Jian Xu
papers.summary: Shown the same feed, the same user might scroll to item 20 and click two things this time, and leave at item 8 the next; the log keeps only one of these. BrowseFlow argues that a user simulator should learn the distribution of such outcomes rather than copy that one log. It splits a browsing session into two things, how deep the user scrolls and at which positions they click or like, and generates those key events directly instead of predicting a long run of scroll actions step by step. This matters because in Taobao browsing data only 5.48% of actions are positive feedback such as clicks. On three datasets, its generated sessions come closest to real ones both in overall distribution and in click-count distribution.

papers.title: Beyond IPS: Reliable Counterfactual Evaluation in Multi-Stage Ad Systems without Logged Propensities
papers.authors: Mohsen Malmir, Mohamed A. Radwan, Houssam Nassif, Murat Ali Bayir
papers.summary: Before an ad system launches a new ranking model, it must pick the best candidate offline from logs. In multi-stage delivery, impressions pass through auctions, filters and caching, and their selection probabilities are never logged, so IPS cannot be used. The usual substitute scores new policies with a click-predicting reward model, but new policies push impressions toward ads that are rare in the logs, where that model is least accurate. The authors replay the candidates on past requests and train a classifier to tell whether an impression comes from the logs or from a given candidate. For each logged impression, the classifier gives the ratio of its probability under each candidate to its probability under the logs. The average of these ratios over all candidates becomes its weight when training one shared reward model, so impressions that look like what the candidates would show count more. Five candidates in a production CTR ranking system all ran in A/B tests. Picking a winner on each of 50 random log subsamples, the rate of picking the truly best one rises from 0.36 without weighting to 0.40.

papers.title: WeSearch: A Unified Model-Centric Retrieval Framework for WeChat Search
papers.authors: Kepu Zhang, Yuzhe Cai, Yue Shu, Dawei Chen, Jinhai Zhu, Yuan Xu, Zehua Dai, Tongke Ni, Ziyao Chen, Chen Fu, Jie Shao, Ch...
papers.summary: WeSearch at WeChat Search replaces the old set of parallel retrieval paths with one model: it first finds the document clusters relevant to the query, then scores individual documents inside those clusters, separating coarse pruning from fine relevance judgment. Unlike generative retrieval, it does not give each document one fixed hierarchical Semantic ID; that approach assumes a document follows a single semantic path, while many articles cover several topics at once. The index updates incrementally, so the model moves from monthly updates to weekly refreshes, or daily when needed. It is now the main retrieval path of WeChat Search, and a month-long full-traffic A/B test showed CTR up 0.68% and retrieval resource cost down 41%. ==Take more clusters to protect recall, and leave relevance to per-document scoring==.

papers.title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
papers.authors: Sedigheh Eslami, Markus Krimmel, William Barber, Antoine Chaffin, Maximilian Schall, Jonas Golde, Louis Milliken, Ekater...
papers.summary: Contextual embeddings are trained and evaluated as if a question had only one relevant chunk in a document, and this paper shows that assumption fails in RAG. Answering a question often also needs the chunks that say which product or which year the answer is about, yet current training treats every chunk of the same document other than the answer chunk as a negative, so these supporting chunks get pushed down. The authors use an existing context compression model as the teacher. Its normal job is to pick out the parts of a retrieved document relevant to the query, and it gives every token a relevance score. Each chunk's score is the mean of its top few token scores, and the embedding model learns to match it, so no answer-chunk labels are needed. On a new diagnostic benchmark, the 9B model finds the answer in its top 10 chunks for 45.5% of queries, against 31.1% for the strongest baseline, voyage-context-4.

papers.title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
papers.authors: Hira Naveed, Scott Barnett, Stefanus Kurniawan, John Grundy, Chetan Arora, Hourieh Khalajzadeh, Omar Haggag
papers.summary: RAGLog reads only the API logs each run of a RAG pipeline leaves behind, with no reference answers and no code changes, and points out which stage of the run went wrong. This matters because a pipeline can go wrong in the middle and still give the right final answer. Across natural runs of five open-source pipelines, 37% had at least one faulty stage, and more than a third of those still answered correctly, so checking the answer alone misses them. It checks each stage in turn: whether the rewritten query dropped names, numbers or dates from the question, whether any retrieved passage actually contains the answer, whether reranking pushed the passage with the answer out, and whether the answer is backed by the context. A classifier trained for each stage then decides whether that stage is faulty. On naturally occurring faults it finds the faulty stage with an F1 of 0.73, against 0.58 for Claude Code. ==For debugging RAG, the logs alone are enough for a first pass.==

papers.title: DR Pixel: Page-Native Deep Research with Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Tiansheng Hu, Yichuan Wang, James V. Talwar, Nicholas Tomlin, Chen Zhao, Sewon Min
papers.summary: Letting a research agent read page screenshots, instead of first converting PDFs to text and searching that, raises question-answering accuracy and needs fewer searches. DR Pixel renders about 1.06 million paper pages as images and encodes each image as one vector. The agent issues text queries, gets back the most relevant page images, and keeps looking at these original images for the whole trajectory, so tables and curves are never distorted by text conversion. With no training at all, just switching to pages, three closed and open models all gain more than 5 points over converting PDFs to text plus a separate figure-search tool, while making 20% to 30% fewer retrieval calls.

papers.title: Every Clause Counts: Instruction-Following Reranking by Multiplying Small, Answerable Questions
papers.authors: S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed, Abdullah Al Musaddiq
papers.summary: A search reranker can respect the requirements users attach to their queries without training any parameters: written for beginners, in a certain language, official sources only. DMReranker splits an instructed query into a topic and a few concrete conditions, lets a small model answer one narrow question per condition, and multiplies the probabilities that each condition is met into one score. The WISE score of the InfoSearch benchmark checks whether documents that meet a requirement move up when it is added and move down under the opposite one. GPT-4o used as a reranker averages only 33.5 WISE, while DMReranker reaches 50.9. ==If any requirement is clearly unmet, the total score is pushed far down==.

papers.title: Re$^3$Rank: Listwise Reranking with Reasoning-Conditioned Retrieval Heads
papers.authors: Ruiyi Yan, Zhuoyuan Mao, Yugo Murawaki, Yiwen Guo
papers.summary: Re3Rank changes what looks at the candidates in attention-based reranking: one model first reads the question and candidates and writes a reasoning trace, then a second model looks with the trace's tokens and ranks candidates by the attention they receive. Existing methods look with the question's own tokens, but the question often lacks the key clues needed to find the evidence. Across 9 QA datasets, the 4B version averages 76.70 R@3, 3.31 points above QRRanker, also at 4B. ==What decides the ranking is what does the looking at candidates==.

papers.title: Characterizing Adversarial GEO via Implicit Brand Injection
papers.authors: Shobhnik Kriplani, Haohan Wang
papers.summary: Quietly adding one sentence that mentions a brand to a web article can be enough to get that brand into a generative search engine's answer. The authors split the job across a team of agents that pick where to insert, rewrite that sentence, check that the edit reads naturally, and choose among several candidates, then test it on a set of web articles and made-up brands. The edited articles do not read like ads, yet they are retrieved more often: the edited passage lands in the top 10 results up to 82.2% of the time, and the generated answer mentions the brand up to 62.7% of the time. ==A single soft placement moves both retrieval and the answer, so generative search needs defenses against it.==

papers.title: QueryFlow: Multi-Hop Graph Retrieval with Adaptive Query Evolution
papers.authors: Manzong Huang, Chenyang Bu, Yi He, Jiapu Wang, Xindong Wu
papers.summary: The paper builds a multi-hop graph retriever, QueryFlow, that revises the question as it searches. After each propagation layer, it condenses the context found so far into a summary vector, merges it into the question state, and uses the new state to steer how the next layer searches. Earlier graph retrievers such as GFM-RAG keep the original question as the condition throughout propagation. Yet in multi-hop QA, some evidence looks irrelevant to the original question until an intermediate fact has been found. On four multi-hop QA datasets, compared with GFM-RAG, the share of questions whose top 10 results contain all needed evidence rises by 8.40 percentage points on average, and LLM answer accuracy rises by 11.6 percentage points. ==A question state that updates with what is already known finds complete evidence more often than a fixed question.==

papers.title: Scaling Laws For Data-Constrained Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Bowen Fu, Jingtao Zhan
papers.summary: Labeled data for dense retrieval is usually limited, so it gets reused for many epochs. In that situation, should you buy a bigger pretrained model or collect more labels? The authors fine-tuned 35 BERT-family retrievers on MS MARCO subsets of different sizes and recorded the lowest evaluation loss each combination reaches during training. That minimum is fitted accurately by a power law that multiplies parameter count and unique samples, better than the usual additive form; the learning rate mainly changes how fast the minimum is reached, not how low it goes. By the fitted law, for the same fine-tuning compute, a larger pretrained model lowers this loss about 1.46 times as much as more in-domain data does. ==When data is limited, a bigger model is usually the better buy.==

papers.title: DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
papers.authors: Dingyi Kang, Bingzhe Li
papers.summary: The work that multi-hop question answering piles onto one LLM can be split up. In this paper's DeFT-RAG, the LLM writes one sub-question at a time that names every entity it asks about. A program records each sub-question and its answer in a QA table by fixed rules, and the LLM reads this table at the end to answer the original question. On MuSiQue, accuracy rises from the strongest baseline's 0.577 to 0.629. Because each sub-question names its entities in full, answers can also be reused across questions: 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache and LLM calls drop by 12.9%, with no loss in accuracy. Multi-hop questions are hard because evidence must be found link by link through intermediate entities the question never names. Iterative methods make the LLM plan, order, rewrite and keep track at once, and each task fails in its own way.

papers.title: TableTune: Measured, Self-Correcting Draft-Length Tables for Dynamic Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Abhishek Malvankar, Paul Castro, Nick Mitchell, Lionel Villard
papers.summary: The table in vLLM's documentation that sets how many tokens speculative decoding guesses per step at each batch size can visibly cut throughput on a different GPU or model. This paper gives a tool that measures the best table in minutes and keeps correcting it as traffic changes. Speculation only pays while the GPU has spare compute, so the more requests share a batch, the fewer tokens each step should guess. TableTune times every batch size and draft length on vLLM's own serving path and picks the highest-throughput table. Once in production, a plugin reads vLLM's counts of accepted guesses, combines them with the measured step times, and rewrites the table with the length that yields the most useful tokens per second at each batch size. On a mixture-of-experts model, against the fastest fixed draft length at each load, the documented table is up to 18% slower and the measured table at most 3% slower.

papers.title: Modular and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search with Vectorium and kANNolo
papers.authors: Silvio Martinico, Franco Maria Nardini, Cosimo Rulli, Rossano Venturini
papers.summary: In vector search, switching to another embedding form or quantizer often means switching libraries. Existing ANN libraries either support one combination or write separate code for each, and none covers dense, sparse and multi-vector embeddings together. Vectorium and kANNolo are two open-source Rust libraries: the first handles vectors, distances and quantization, and the second builds HNSW and IVF indexes on top. Every combination is compiled into specialized code, so splitting things into modules costs no run-time speed. In 12 comparisons on dense data, they give the best memory and throughput trade-off in 9. A team running both dense and sparse retrieval no longer needs a different library for each quantizer or index.

papers.title: Look Before You Launch: Learned Throughput Prediction for Hardware Selection in a Production Training Fleet
papers.authors: Hossein Askari, Wei Sun, Chenguang Zhu, Bin Zan, Sreen Tallam, Keyu Man
papers.summary: The same training job can often run on several accelerator types, and which one is cheapest depends on its throughput on each. A job placed on the wrong type still finishes without any error, so the extra cost goes unnoticed. LEAP, a hardware-selection service the authors run in a production fleet, predicts a job's throughput on every candidate type at submission time, then ranks the types by predicted throughput per unit cost, choosing hardware for tens of thousands of training jobs a day. 77% of its predictions land within 20% of the measured throughput. After six months it ranked 95% of the eligible training GPU-hours, and the authors estimate it saves about 3% of training compute cost.

papers.title: FlatCake: A Flat KVCache Storage Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Xin Huang, Teng Ma, Zhuoran Li, Yibo Zhao, Zhaoshi Li, Qianchao Zhu, Wei Yang, Chenxi Wang, Tao Xie, Youwei Zhuo
papers.summary: After analyzing eight production LLM request traces, the authors find that the common practice of treating host memory as a KV cache layer in front of the SSD barely filters any reads under these workloads. Reused blocks either come back only after a long gap, or belong to agent sessions of several gigabytes each that memory cannot hold, so the SSD always ends up on the read path. FlatCake puts memory and SSD at the same level and decides each block's home when it is created. Shared system prompts and short-reply chats go to memory, while multi-gigabyte agent sessions are written straight to the SSD. A session's blocks are stored contiguously and never move, and reads stream large chunks from the SSD straight into the GPU. Replaying a production Claude Code trace, the share of prefixes it reads back instead of recomputing holds at 94% as load rises, while Mooncake drops to 64%. KV storage for long agent sessions should be planned per session.

papers.title: AttentionIndex: Accelerating Learned Sparse Attention with a Causal Inverted-File Index
papers.authors: Jeongmin Brian Park, Wen-mei Hwu
papers.summary: In learned sparse attention, as used by DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3, each query attends to only k keys, but the small scoring network that picks those k keys still scores every key in the prefix. At one million tokens, that step takes more than half of prefill time. AttentionIndex sharply cuts this cost. During prefill it groups keys by similarity; a query first scores one representative per group, and only the members of the most promising groups go to the original scoring network for the final pick. At that length, its prefill throughput is 1.3 to 1.8 times that of scoring every key, and it misses fewer keys than HiSA, a block-based method at similar speed.

papers.title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
papers.authors: Hamidreza Alikhani, Nazmul Takbir, Matin Khajavi, Rajat Bhattacharjya, Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi, Nikil Dutt
papers.summary: Prefill queueing under a prefix cache can keep both the median latency low and the tail short. While the queue is short, serve cheap requests with long cache hits first; move a request forward the longer it has waited relative to its own prefill time; and cap how much work cheap requests may place ahead of the oldest request. This is what Fairway does. Agent and RAG requests often share a prefix, so the remaining work of requests in one queue can differ by about 100 times, and the serving order decides how long each request waits for its first token. In traffic spikes, Fairway's median time to first token is 0.82 seconds with a p99 close to first-come-first-served, while hit-leaning orderings let the p99 reach 11 to 50 seconds.

papers.title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs
papers.authors: Dongfang Zhao
papers.summary: For high-recall vector search on GPUs, graph search is held back by its chain of dependent rounds, not by distance computation itself. OctEx spends GPU memory on neighbor lists precomputed at build time. It makes a few hundred randomly projected low-dimensional copies of the data, cuts each copy into grid cells, and stores for every cell a list of the vectors closest to its center. A query computes which cell it falls into in each copy, reads those lists in one parallel step to get candidates, then reads the stored neighbor tables of the best few candidates for a fixed few rounds. Against CAGRA, the standard GPU graph-search baseline, it is 2.0 to 46.4 times faster at high recall on seven datasets of up to one hundred million vectors. On billion-vector datasets, the gain shrinks to 1.46 to 2.05 times. ==Trading GPU memory for serial waiting at query time is the core trade-off of this paper.==

papers.title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
papers.authors: Chengzhi Lu, Boxi Zhou, Yanying Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov
papers.summary: A ten-minute traffic surge can leave an agent serving engine with prefill and decode disaggregated unable to recover. After the surge ends and traffic returns to a level the engine handled before, goodput on SGLang stays about 88% lower over the following hour, and ==utilization and queue length give almost no warning beforehand.== Behind it is a loop: too little cache causes recomputation, calls slow down, sessions end later, more context is live at once, and the cache falls even shorter. Based on this, the authors build Basin. It reserves each session's predicted largest context from a total budget and queues new sessions when the budget runs out. On real GPUs, a simplified prototype without the predictor already reaches 1.20 to 1.70 times the goodput of Continuum, the strongest prior system.

papers.title: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
papers.authors: Kunming Shao, Xijie Huang, Jierun Chen, Jiaqi Shao, Yanli Wang, Jiangnan Yu, Qiwei Li, Wei Zhang, Kwang-Ting Cheng, Chi ...
papers.summary: Long-context inference is bound by the KV cache, and squeezing keys to very few bits would save a lot of memory if the error stays small. The usual fix rotates keys before quantizing, assuming rotation always helps. The authors find it does not: rotation flattens a spiky piece of a key but can give a flat piece a new spike, and both kinds often sit in the same key. FlagRot therefore cuts each key into small pieces and, on calibration data, checks whether rotating each piece gives a smaller error in the attention scores; it stores the piece in whichever form wins. At read time it rotates only the matching parts of the query, so the scores come out as if nothing had been rotated. At 2.5 bits per value on average, it lowers the KL divergence between the common KIVI quantizer and the original model from 18.7 to 12.4, averaged over 12 models.

papers.title: Testing Processor Contracts in Speculative Decoding Engines
papers.authors: Tianyu Ding, Yaocheng Tong, Muzhi Yang, Lei Yang, Fei Jiang
papers.summary: Speculative decoding is said to leave the output distribution unchanged, but that guarantee has a precondition. Components that change token scores, such as grammar constraints, repetition penalties and watermarks, are called logits processors, and at every verification position they must receive the right prefix and state. The authors examined selected releases of Transformers and llama-cpp-python and confirmed two failure modes: a processor reads draft tokens that have not been verified yet, or it advances its internal state and does not roll it back when the draft is rejected. On one trained model with classifier-free guidance, the authors pick one prompt and count whether the first output token is a token fixed in advance. Between ordinary decoding and speculative decoding that drafts from the prompt, that probability differs by at least 60.26 percentage points. When speculative decoding speeds up constrained generation, the output may already have changed without anyone noticing.

papers.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
papers.authors: Yueh-Hua Wu, Kei Ota, Hanlong Li, Hayata Yuasa, Jason Wang, Kengo Ikeuchi, Kensuke Chiyoma, Makoto Sugiura, Masafumi Tak...
papers.summary: Robot imitation learning usually starts with teleoperating a robot to collect data; AIRoA-0 collects no robot data at all. It is trained only on 16,151 hours of bimanual demonstrations that people recorded with a handheld gripper, and the robot shows up only at test time. At a site where none of its training data was recorded, using just one camera on each wrist, it sorts small parts, swaps the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum, folds a towel and more, averaging 78% success over ten tasks. Post-trained on the same task demonstrations, the best of four other vision-language-action models (VLAs) reaches only 27%. Data collection no longer has to be tied to one robot: any robot that mounts the same gripper can run the model.

papers.title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
papers.authors: Shresth Grover, Andrey Kolobov, Dhruv Shah
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a generalist vision-language-action model (VLA) on a few demonstrations of one task makes it better at that task, but it then fails more easily when the object, background or wording changes. RAFT splits post-training into two steps: it first trains a set of LoRA adapters on data annotated with task-relevant reasoning, such as which objects and regions matter, then freezes them and fine-tunes the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, success in situations unseen during training rises from 27.9% with plain fine-tuning to 75.0%. The resulting policy also attends more to task-relevant regions: teaching it where to look before teaching actions loses much less generalization.

papers.title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
papers.authors: Zhixuan Xu, Yichen Li, Bingchen Wu, Rui Wang, Yiwen Hou, Zixuan Liu, Tianyu Qiu, Lin Shao
papers.summary: Teaching a robot hand from human demonstrations is hard because human and robot hands have different shapes. If the conversion only tries to make the robot hand look like the human hand, the robot's fingertips often touch the object in different places than the human did, and grasps and pushes fail. CIMI puts contact first. During demonstrations it records the contact surfaces between fingers and object plus fingertip camera views; when converting to robot motion it aligns the contact points first and the finger pose second. The learned policy likewise predicts how the contact surface should move next, and a controller coordinates wrist and fingers to match it. Across six hand-task pairs on the LEAP and Wuji hands, mean full-task success beats baseline policies by at least 50 percentage points. ==When transferring human skills, matching contact matters more than matching hand shape==.

papers.title: LeRobot:  An Open-Source Library for End-to-End Robot Learning
papers.authors: Remi Cadene, Simon Alibert, Francesco Capuano, Michel Aractingi, Adil Zouitine, Pepijn Kooijmans, Jade Choghari, Martino...
papers.summary: The robot learning toolchain is fragmented: motor communication, data collection, dataset formats, training algorithms and deployment each tend to use their own stack, so switching robots or datasets means re-assembling everything, and other people's results are hard to reproduce. LeRobot puts the whole chain into one open-source library: low-level motor control and support for low-cost hardware, a unified dataset format with streaming, implementations of several mainstream policy algorithms, and asynchronous inference. Its value is not a new algorithm but letting data and results from different labs be compared and reused within one set of tools.

papers.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
papers.authors: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang, Amish Sethi
papers.summary: Most of the training data came from handheld grippers, collected at a different place and under different lighting than the test scene, with only a small share of real-robot teleoperation. Fine-tuned on this mix, pi0.5 succeeded in all 10 trials of a bimanual task that puts oranges into a bowl. The demonstrations come from UMI-Live, an open-source bimanual handheld data-collection system released with the paper. The camera, LiDAR, compute and battery are packed into the gripper, the operator presses one button to record the next take, and a background pipeline turns finished takes into training-ready data. ==UMI-Live's value is not a new algorithm but a data-collection pipeline you can actually reproduce==, and the authors also release about 40 hours of data.

papers.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Ammar N. Abbas, Aayush Jain, Prashanth Viswanath, Nivesh Gadipudi, Giulia Vilone, Jim Gibbons
papers.summary: A low validation loss does not mean an imitation-learning policy works on the real robot. The authors had a five-fingered robot hand grasp and insert an RJ45 network connector and tested 281 policies on hardware to find which design choices actually decide success. The answer: how observations and actions are represented matters far more than the optimizer or sampling scheme. For point-cloud policies, keeping only the region around the target and expressing the points in the robot-base frame each raised success by 70 to 100 percentage points. Among dozens of offline metrics, only a few measuring whether predicted motion is smooth and direct correlated clearly with insertion success, and only within a single policy family. ==Offline metrics cannot yet replace real-robot testing==.

papers.title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
papers.authors: Sombit Dey, Luc Van Gool, Danda Pani Paudel
papers.summary: As VLAs grow, every action waits for the large model to finish, so the robot reacts slowly. ARP runs the two jobs separately at their own pace: the large VLM refreshes its understanding of the task and scene every so often, which the paper calls semantic memory, while a small vision-action model reads that memory and outputs actions at a high rate. Because the large model's view always lags a little, the small model is told at every step how old the memory is and how long its own actions will be delayed. During training it is also deliberately fed older memories, so it learns to act well despite the mismatch. On a Franka arm, compared with conventional VLA baselines, it succeeds more often and finishes tasks in 20% less time. The large model need not be present at every step: running the VLM at a tenth of its usual frequency costs almost nothing.

papers.title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization for Agentic Robotics
papers.authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang...
papers.summary: Frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra can already control robots directly and generalize better than VLAs. The authors argue this ability splits into two skills: understanding what a task asks for, and actually moving the robot. Small open VLMs already have the first and mainly lack the second. ZAP teaches that missing skill entirely in simulation, on simple primitive tasks, using the model's own successful attempts, with no real-robot data and no distillation from a frontier model. On real-world tasks it reaches 96.7% success, matching GPT-6 Astra, while each task costs one seventeenth as much to run. By training only the missing skill, a small model gets close to a frontier one.

papers.title: ReGATE: Recurrent Gated Visual Fusion for Reactive Humanoid-Object Interaction
papers.authors: Hao Zhu, Jorge Peña-Queralta
papers.summary: When a humanoid robot reaches for a box, the box blocks its head depth camera as soon as the hands get close, yet the controller still has to finish the whole sequence of picking up, carrying and putting down. This paper lets the robot act mainly through the joint-state pathway and treats the depth image only as a correction scaled by learned gates, designed to let less of it in when the image is unreliable. Information gathered over earlier frames is kept in the memory of recurrent layers, so it is not lost the moment the image drops out. In simulation it picks up static boxes 85.2% of the time, against 48.5% for VisualMimic under the same protocol. On a real Unitree G1, after the camera saw the box once and was then completely covered, the robot still grasped the box. ==When the view can be blocked, relying mainly on joint states and taking in the image as needed is steadier.==

papers.title: DexHOT: Learning Hand-Object Configuration Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
papers.authors: Zhewei Gui, Anthony Bolton, Jiyao Zhang, Zeyuan Chen, Qiyang Yan, Tianyu Wang, Hao Dong
papers.summary: Dexterous manipulation is not only about moving an object somewhere; the fingers must keep holding it in a useful way so the next action can follow. Many methods specify only the object's target pose and leave the grasp to the policy. DexHOT writes the goal directly as the hand's joint posture plus the object's position relative to the wrist, so the policy learns to move from one grasp configuration to the next, and long tasks become a chain of such subgoals. All training data is synthetic, with no human reference motions. Across 120 objects, a single policy succeeds 80.5% of the time on seen objects and 69.4% on unseen ones.
